newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Canada's Placer exits from Philippine copper mine.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Placer exits from Philippine copper mine.

text.p: Canada's Placer Dome Inc on Friday announced it was divesting its 39.9 percent stake in a Philipppine copper mine that has been shut since a major leak of tailings last year.
"Placer Dome has transferred to Marcopper Mining Corporation of the Philippines Placer Dome's 39.9 percent shareholding in the company," Placer Dome said in a statement issued in Manila.
Placer Dome will not receive any compensation for the shares it transfers to Marcopper's majority owners F Holdings, a private company controlled by the Bernadino family.

The accident in March last year at the copper mine located in Marinduque, 160 km (100 miles) south of Manila, caused a furore in the Philippines with several environmental groups demanding tougher safety measures.
The leak in a tunnel of the mine was estimated to have dumped 1.5 million cubic metres of tailings, or mine waste, and affected wide stretches of the 25 km (15.5 mile) Boac river.
Placer Dome said the leak was not toxic and there was no immediate danger to human health.

"We are withdrawing from Marcopper under an arrangement consistent with our values. This divestiture results from our lack of majority control of Marcopper, the differing priorities of the shareholder groups and the fact that Placer Dome no longer focuses on copper," the statement quoted Placer Dome chief executive John Willson as saying.
Willson said the move in no way affected Placer Dome's commitment to mitigate the effects of the tailings spill from the Marcopper mine into the Boac river.
The statement said Placer Dome continued to provide money to settle more than 2,000 claims for about 19 million pesos ($722,000) from people in 44 villages affected by the spill.
It said Placer Dome is continuing to clean up the river and less than 30 percent of the tailings remains on its banks.
Last year, Placer wrote off its investment in Marcopper and took a $43 million charge to earnings for the accident.
Two Placer executives at Marcopper face criminal charges for the spill.

One of the executives, John Loney, who was then president of Marcopper Mining, told Reuters that Placer's exit from the Marinduque mine was not influenced by the accident but was decided two years ago.
"This was because we are getting out of copper and moving into gold," Loney, who is now president of Placer Pacific Asia Pte Ltd, said.
Placer would repair the tunnel which sprang the leak, clean up the river and "enable Marcopper to get on with the business", Loney said.
Placer was one of the original shareholders in the Marcopper mine which was started in 1964.
Loney said with the company's exit from Marcopper, it had no more mining interests in the Philippines. But it continued to be involved in exploration, he said, without giving details.
